entries.1:1: This sets the scene in the huge empire of King Ahasuerus, which stretched from India to Ethiopia. It reminds the reader that this story happens in a real place under a very powerful ruler.
entries.1:2: At this time the king was ruling from his palace in the city of Shushan. The story is anchored in his royal capital.
entries.1:3: In the third year of his reign the king threw a big banquet for his officials and military leaders. He was showing off his power to the people who served him.
entries.1:4: The king displayed his vast wealth and splendor for six months. He wanted everyone to see how rich and important he was.
entries.1:5: After that, he held a seven-day feast for everyone living in the city, rich and poor alike, in the palace garden. He made sure even ordinary people got to share in the celebration.
entries.1:6: The garden was lavishly decorated with fine fabrics, silver and marble, and gold and silver couches. The extreme luxury shows how wealthy and extravagant the king was.
entries.1:7: Drinks were served in gold cups, each one different, with plenty of royal wine. The king was generous with his riches.
entries.1:8: Guests could drink as much or as little as they wanted, because the king had ordered that no one be pressured. He wanted people to enjoy themselves freely.
entries.1:9: Queen Vashti also held a separate banquet for the women in the palace. She had her own role in hosting the royal celebration.
entries.1:10: On the last day, when the king was feeling merry from wine, he summoned seven of his personal servants. A tipsy king was about to make a rash demand.
entries.1:11: He ordered Queen Vashti to come wearing her crown so everyone could admire her beauty. He wanted to show her off like one of his treasures.
entries.1:12: Vashti refused to come, and the king flew into a furious rage. Her refusal set off a serious crisis in the royal court.
entries.1:13: The king consulted his wise advisers who knew the laws and customs. He wanted a legal ruling on what to do about his wife's refusal.
entries.1:14: These advisers were the seven highest officials in the empire and the king's closest friends. The most powerful men in the land were deciding Vashti's fate.
entries.1:15: The king asked his advisers what the law said should be done to a queen who disobeyed his direct command. He was looking for official justification for punishing her.
entries.1:16: Memucan answered that Vashti had wronged not just the king but all the officials and people of the empire. He turned a personal quarrel into a public crisis.
entries.1:17: He argued that other women would hear what the queen did and start disrespecting their own husbands. He feared her example would spread disobedience through the whole empire.
entries.1:18: He warned that the wives of Persian and Median officials would soon copy the queen and talk back to their husbands. This would cause widespread shame and anger, he claimed.
entries.1:19: Memucan advised the king to issue an unchangeable royal decree that Vashti could never come before him again and that another woman would take her place. He wanted a permanent, official punishment.
entries.1:20: He said that once this decree was announced across the vast empire, all wives would respect their husbands. He promised the decree would fix the problem everywhere.
entries.1:21: The king and his officials liked this advice, so the king did what Memucan suggested. The queen was condemned on the strength of one adviser's argument.
entries.1:22: The king sent letters to every province in its own script and language declaring that every man should be master of his own household. The decree was broadcast to the whole empire in terms everyone could understand.
entries.2:1: The king had calmed down but started remembering Vashti and the order he had made against her. It shows how a rash decision can keep troubling someone long after the anger fades.
entries.2:2: The king's servants suggested finding beautiful young women for him. They were trying to solve the king's problem by offering a practical plan.
entries.2:3: The plan was to gather beautiful young women from across the kingdom into the royal women's house in Susa, under Hegai's care, and give them beauty treatments. It shows how the king's word could reach every part of his empire.
entries.2:4: The girl the king liked best would become queen instead of Vashti, and the king agreed to this plan. A personal loss was being turned into a kingdom-wide search.
entries.2:5: Mordecai, a Jew from the tribe of Benjamin, was living in Susa, the capital city. This introduces a key person in the story.
entries.2:6: Mordecai's family had been taken from Jerusalem as captives when Babylon's king defeated Judah. His background is one of exile and loss.
entries.2:7: Mordecai raised his orphaned cousin Esther as his own daughter because she had no parents, and she was very beautiful. He took responsibility for her when she had no one else.
entries.2:8: When the king's order was announced, many girls were brought to the palace, and Esther was taken there too and placed under Hegai's care. She had no choice in being taken.
entries.2:9: Hegai liked Esther and gave her special treatment, beauty supplies, her rightful gifts, seven maids, and the best rooms. She found favor with the person in charge.
entries.2:10: Esther kept her family and nationality a secret because Mordecai had told her to. She followed his advice even in the palace.
entries.2:11: Mordecai walked by the women's courtyard every day to check on Esther and find out how she was doing. He kept watching over her like a caring parent.
entries.2:12: Each girl had to go through twelve months of beauty treatments before her turn with the king. It shows how long and elaborate the preparation was.
entries.2:13: When a girl's turn came, she could take whatever she wanted from the women's house to the king's house. She was allowed to bring things that might help her.
entries.2:14: A girl went to the king in the evening and was moved to a different house the next day, only returning if the king specifically asked for her by name. This shows how little control the women had over their own lives.
entries.2:15: When Esther's turn came, she asked for nothing beyond what Hegai advised, and everyone who saw her liked her. Her humility and good judgment made a strong impression.
entries.2:16: Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus in the tenth month of the seventh year of his reign. The story gives a precise date for this important moment.
entries.2:17: The king loved Esther more than any other woman and made her queen instead of Vashti. She rose from being a captive's relative to becoming queen.
entries.2:18: The king held a great banquet in Esther's honor, gave a holiday throughout the provinces, and handed out gifts. He celebrated his new queen publicly and generously.
entries.2:19: When the young women were gathered a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate. He had found a place near the palace where he could stay close to Esther.
entries.2:20: Esther still kept her family and nationality secret, just as Mordecai had instructed, and she continued to obey him as she had when she lived with him. She stayed loyal to his guidance even as queen.
entries.2:21: Two of the king's doorkeepers, Bigthan and Teresh, became angry and looked for a chance to attack King Ahasuerus. A plot against the king was forming right inside the palace.
entries.2:22: Mordecai found out about the plot and told Esther, who reported it to the king in Mordecai's name. Mordecai's alertness saved the king's life.
entries.2:23: The plot was investigated, found to be true, and the two men were hanged, and the whole event was written down in the royal records. The good deed was recorded, even though no reward is mentioned yet.
entries.3:1: The king promoted Haman to a rank above all his other officials. This shows how quickly power can be handed to someone who will later use it to harm others.
entries.3:2: Everyone else bowed to Haman because the king commanded it, but Mordecai refused. Mordecai's choice to disobey set up the conflict that follows.
entries.3:3: The other servants asked Mordecai why he was breaking the king's command. They noticed his refusal and pressed him about it.
entries.3:4: Mordecai kept refusing day after day, so they reported him to Haman to see if he would get away with it, since he had told them he was a Jew. His identity became the reason his defiance mattered.
entries.3:5: When Haman saw that Mordecai would not bow, he became furious. His anger shows how much he valued being honored by everyone.
entries.3:6: Haman decided that punishing only Mordecai was not enough, and he plotted to destroy all the Jews throughout the kingdom. One man's refusal turned into a plan to wipe out a whole people.
entries.3:7: They cast lots, called Pur, to pick the right day for the plan, and the lot fell on a day in the twelfth month. The timing was decided by chance, yet the story shows it was not outside God's control.
entries.3:8: Haman told the king that the Jews were scattered everywhere, had different laws, and did not obey the king's laws, so they should not be tolerated. He twisted their distinctness into a reason to destroy them.
entries.3:9: Haman asked the king to issue a written order to destroy the Jews and offered a huge sum of silver for the royal treasury. He was willing to pay to carry out his hatred.
entries.3:10: The king took off his signet ring and gave it to Haman, handing him the authority to act. The king gave power to a man who hated the Jews.
entries.3:11: The king told Haman to keep the money and do whatever he wanted with the people. The king gave no real thought to the fate of an entire people.
entries.3:12: On the thirteenth day of the first month, the king's scribes wrote out Haman's orders in every language and sealed them with the king's ring. The plan became official law across the empire.
entries.3:13: The letters ordered the killing of all Jews, young and old, men, women, and children, on one day, and the seizing of their property. This was a decree for genocide, not just punishment.
entries.3:14: Copies of the decree were published everywhere so people could prepare for that day. The whole empire was put on notice about the coming slaughter.
entries.3:15: The messengers hurried out, and while the king and Haman drank together, the city of Shushan was confused and alarmed. The contrast shows how careless the powerful were while ordinary people sensed the danger.
entries.4:1: Mordecai was so upset by the order to kill the Jews that he tore his clothes, put on rough sackcloth, and wailed loudly in the city. His grief shows how seriously he took the threat, and it invites us to grieve honestly when something terrible happens.
entries.4:2: He stopped at the king's gate because no one in mourning clothes was allowed inside. This shows the danger and the strict rules of the palace, and how Mordecai's sorrow kept him shut out from where help could be found.
entries.4:3: Wherever the king's order reached, Jews everywhere mourned, wept, fasted, and lay in sackcloth and ashes. The whole people shared the same fear and sorrow, showing that grief is often felt together, not alone.
entries.4:4: When Esther heard about Mordecai, she was deeply upset and sent him proper clothes to replace his sackcloth, but he refused them. She cared about him, yet his refusal showed her that this was far more serious than just his personal distress.
entries.4:5: Esther sent her trusted servant Hathach to find out exactly what had happened and why Mordecai was acting this way. She wanted the facts before deciding what to do, which is a wise first step when trouble comes.
entries.4:6: Hathach went out to the open square in front of the king's gate where Mordecai was. He went to Mordecai directly, so the message could pass between them.
entries.4:7: Mordecai told Hathach everything that had happened, including the huge sum of money Haman promised to pay for the Jews' destruction. He held nothing back, so Esther would understand how deadly the situation really was.
entries.4:8: Mordecai gave Hathach a copy of the death order and urged Esther to go to the king, beg for mercy, and plead for her people. He was asking her to risk everything to help others, not just to save herself.
entries.4:9: Hathach returned and told Esther everything Mordecai had said. The message reached her clearly, leaving her to decide how she would respond.
entries.4:10: Esther then sent Hathach back to Mordecai with her reply. She was about to explain why going to the king was not as simple as he thought.
entries.4:11: Esther explained that anyone who went to the king without being invited could be put to death unless he held out his gold scepter, and she had not been called for thirty days. Her life was genuinely at risk, so Mordecai's request was far more dangerous than it sounded.
entries.4:12: Hathach passed Esther's words on to Mordecai. The two of them were now fully aware of the danger on both sides.
entries.4:13: Mordecai warned Esther not to think she would escape just because she lived in the palace. Being close to power does not protect you when danger comes to your whole people.
entries.4:14: Mordecai said that if Esther stayed silent, help would come from somewhere else, but she and her family would be lost, and perhaps she became queen for exactly this moment. He challenged her to see her position as a responsibility, not just a privilege.
entries.4:15: Esther sent her answer back to Mordecai. She had made up her mind and was ready to act.
entries.4:16: Esther asked all the Jews in the city to fast for her for three days and nights, and she and her women would do the same; then she would go to the king even though it was against the law, and if she died, she died. She faced her fear with courage and trusted God through prayer and fasting.
entries.4:17: Mordecai left and did everything Esther had asked. He obeyed her plan, showing that the two of them were now working together in a dangerous but hopeful moment.
entries.5:1: Esther dressed in her royal clothes and stood in the inner courtyard where the king could see her from his throne. She was taking a brave risk by approaching him without being invited, which could mean death.
entries.5:2: The king looked at her with favor and held out his gold scepter, a sign that she was welcome and safe. Esther came close and touched the top of it, showing she accepted his welcome.
entries.5:3: The king asked Esther what she wanted and promised to give it, even up to half his kingdom. He was offering her a very generous open door to make her request.
entries.5:4: Esther didn't blurt out her request yet; she invited the king and Haman to a banquet she had prepared. She was being wise and patient about how she presented her case.
entries.5:5: The king agreed right away and told his servants to bring Haman quickly so they could attend Esther's banquet. Both men came to the meal she had made ready.
entries.5:6: While they drank wine, the king again asked Esther what she wanted and repeated his promise to grant it. He was giving her another clear chance to speak.
entries.5:7: Esther began her answer carefully, introducing what she was about to ask. She was building up to her real request rather than rushing it.
entries.5:8: Esther asked the king and Haman to come to one more banquet the next day, and then she would tell him what she wanted. She was delaying again, perhaps to build tension or wait for the right moment.
entries.5:9: Haman left the banquet happy, but seeing Mordecai refuse to stand or show fear made him furious. One person's disrespect ruined his good mood.
entries.5:10: Haman held back his anger and went home, then called his friends and his wife Zeresh together. He needed people to vent to and to boast before.
entries.5:11: Haman bragged to them about his great wealth, his many children, and how the king had honored and promoted him. He was listing his achievements to impress them.
entries.5:12: Haman boasted that Queen Esther had invited only him to her banquet with the king, and that he was invited again the next day. He was feeling very important and special.
entries.5:13: But Haman admitted that all his success felt worthless as long as he kept seeing Mordecai sitting at the king's gate. One unresolved grievance was eating away at his happiness.
entries.5:14: His wife and friends suggested building a tall pole to hang Mordecai on, and getting the king's permission in the morning so Haman could enjoy the banquet. Haman liked the idea and had the pole made, showing how far his hatred had gone.
entries.6:1: The king couldn't sleep, so he had his official records read to him. God can use small, ordinary events like a sleepless night to set up something bigger.
entries.6:2: The reading turned up the story of how Mordecai had exposed a plot to kill the king. The king learned that a loyal act had been done on his behalf.
entries.6:3: The king asked what reward Mordecai had received, and the answer was nothing. It's a reminder that good deeds can go unnoticed for a while, but they aren't forgotten by God.
entries.6:4: The king asked who was nearby, and it happened to be Haman, who had just arrived to ask permission to hang Mordecai. Haman's plan was about to collide with God's timing.
entries.6:5: The servants told the king that Haman was waiting outside, and the king told them to let him in. Haman had no idea he was walking into a moment that would turn against him.
entries.6:6: The king asked Haman how to honor a man the king wanted to reward, and Haman assumed the man was himself. His pride made him blind to what was really happening.
entries.6:7: Haman began describing the honor he thought should go to the man the king wanted to reward. He was really describing what he wanted for himself.
entries.6:8: Haman suggested the man should wear the king's own robe and ride the king's own horse, with the royal crown on its head. He imagined the highest possible honor.
entries.6:9: Haman said a noble official should lead the honored man through the streets on horseback, announcing his honor to everyone. He pictured himself receiving that public praise.
entries.6:10: The king told Haman to do exactly that for Mordecai the Jew, the very man Haman wanted to kill. Haman was forced to honor his own enemy with his own plan.
entries.6:11: Haman had to dress Mordecai in the royal robes and lead him through the streets announcing his honor. The man who planned a hanging had to publicly praise his target instead.
entries.6:12: Mordecai went back to his post, but Haman hurried home in shame and grief. The tables had turned completely.
entries.6:13: Haman's wife and advisors told him that if Mordecai was Jewish, Haman was doomed to lose. Even his own friends sensed that the tide had turned against him.
entries.6:14: While they were still talking, the king's men arrived to bring Haman to Esther's banquet. Haman had no time to recover before the next turn of events.
entries.7:1: The king and Haman join Esther for a second banquet she had prepared. This sets the scene for her to finally speak up about the danger facing her people.
entries.7:2: The king again urges Esther to tell him what she wants, promising to grant even a huge request. His openness gives her the chance to plead for her life and her people.
entries.7:3: Esther asks the king to spare her life and the lives of her people. She appeals to his favor rather than demanding anything, showing both courage and respect.
entries.7:4: Esther explains that she and her people have been sold to be destroyed and killed. She notes that if they had only been enslaved, she would have stayed quiet, since that would be a smaller loss to the king.
entries.7:5: The king is shocked and asks who would dare do such a thing. He wants to know the person responsible for this evil plan.
entries.7:6: Esther names Haman as the enemy behind the plot, and he is suddenly terrified in front of the king and queen. The accusation turns the tables on him.
entries.7:7: The king storms out to the garden in anger, while Haman stays behind begging Esther to save his life. He realizes the king has turned against him.
entries.7:8: When the king returns, he finds Haman fallen on Esther's couch and accuses him of assaulting the queen. At that moment, attendants cover Haman's face, a sign that he is condemned.
entries.7:9: A servant points out the tall pole Haman had built to hang Mordecai, the man who had helped the king. The king orders Haman to be hanged on it instead.
entries.7:10: Haman is executed on the very pole he made for Mordecai, and the king's anger cools. The plot against God's people collapses on the man who devised it.
entries.8:1: The king gave Esther everything that had belonged to Haman, the man who plotted to kill the Jews. Esther then told the king that Mordecai was her relative, so he was brought into the king's presence.
entries.8:2: The king took back his royal ring from Haman and gave it to Mordecai, giving him Haman's authority. Esther also put Mordecai in charge of Haman's property.
entries.8:3: Esther came to the king again, crying and begging him to stop the evil plan Haman had made to destroy the Jews. She was pleading for the lives of her people.
entries.8:4: The king held out his golden scepter to Esther, a sign that he accepted her and she could speak. So she stood up in front of him.
entries.8:5: Esther asked the king, if he was pleased with her, to send out new letters canceling the orders Haman had sent to destroy the Jews throughout the kingdom. She made her request carefully and respectfully.
entries.8:6: Esther said she could not bear to watch disaster fall on her own people and see them destroyed. Her love for her nation moved her to keep asking for help.
entries.8:7: The king reminded Esther and Mordecai that he had already given Haman's property to Esther and had Haman hanged for attacking the Jews. He was showing he was on their side.
entries.8:8: The king told them to write whatever they wanted about the Jews in his name and seal it with his ring. A letter sealed with the king's ring could not be canceled, so this gave their new order full royal authority.
entries.8:9: The king's secretaries were called on the twenty-third day of the third month, and Mordecai's orders were written down. The letters went to the Jews and to officials in all 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia, each in its own language and script.
entries.8:10: The letters were written in King Ahasuerus's name and sealed with his ring. They were carried by riders on fast royal horses bred for the king's service.
entries.8:11: The king's letters gave Jews in every city the right to gather and defend themselves. They could fight back against any group that attacked them or their families, and they could take the attackers' property.
entries.8:12: The day set for this was the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, called Adar, and it applied in every province of the kingdom.
entries.8:13: A copy of the order was made public in every province so all the peoples would know. This let the Jews be ready on that day to defend themselves against their enemies.
entries.8:14: The riders on the king's fast horses left quickly, urged on by the king's command. The order was also announced in Shushan, the capital city.
entries.8:15: Mordecai left the king's presence wearing royal blue and white robes, a large gold crown, and fine purple and linen clothing. The whole city of Shushan shouted for joy.
entries.8:16: For the Jews, this was a time of light, happiness, and honor after the threat of destruction. Their fear and sadness turned into relief and dignity.
entries.8:17: Wherever the king's letter arrived, the Jews celebrated with joy and feasts. Many people of the land became Jews because they were afraid of the Jews' new power and favor.
entries.9:1: The day that had been set up to destroy the Jews became the day they defeated their enemies instead. It reminds us that plans meant to harm people can be turned around.
entries.9:2: Jews across the empire gathered to defend themselves against anyone who wanted to hurt them, and no one could stand against them because people were afraid of them. It shows that when people unite to protect themselves, fear can shift to their side.
entries.9:3: Officials throughout the kingdom helped the Jews because they were afraid of Mordecai's growing power. It shows how quickly people side with whoever seems to be winning.
entries.9:4: Mordecai had become very powerful in the king's palace, and his reputation spread everywhere as he kept rising. It reminds us that a person's position can change dramatically.
entries.9:5: The Jews defeated all who attacked them and did whatever they wanted to their enemies. It describes a complete victory over those who had tried to harm them.
entries.9:6: In the capital city of Shushan alone, the Jews killed five hundred men. It shows how large the conflict had become.
entries.9:7: This lists the first three of Haman's sons who were killed. It records the specific people who died.
entries.9:8: This continues the list with three more of Haman's sons. It is part of the record of who was killed.
entries.9:9: This names four more of Haman's sons who died. The list keeps track of the family that had plotted against the Jews.
entries.9:10: They killed the ten sons of Haman, the man who had hated the Jews, but they did not take any of their property. It shows they were defending themselves, not looting.
entries.9:11: That same day, the king was told how many people had been killed in the capital. It shows the king was keeping track of what was happening.
entries.9:12: The king told Esther about the deaths in Shushan and asked what else she wanted, promising to grant it. It shows Esther had great influence with the king.
entries.9:13: Esther asked that the Jews in Shushan be allowed one more day to defend themselves and that Haman's ten sons be hanged publicly. She wanted the threat fully ended.
entries.9:14: The king agreed, the order went out, and Haman's ten sons were hanged. It shows the king carrying out Esther's request.
entries.9:15: The Jews in Shushan gathered again on the next day and killed three hundred more men, again without taking their property. It shows the fighting continued one more day in the capital.
entries.9:16: Jews in the rest of the empire defended themselves and killed seventy-five thousand of their enemies, again without taking anything. It shows the scale of the threat they faced and that they fought to survive.
entries.9:17: This happened on the thirteenth day, and on the fourteenth they rested and celebrated with a feast. It marks the day the fighting ended and joy began.
entries.9:18: The Jews in Shushan fought on both the thirteenth and fourteenth, so they rested and celebrated on the fifteenth instead. It explains why their celebration day was different.
entries.9:19: That is why Jews living in small country towns celebrate on the fourteenth day with feasting, joy, and sending gifts to each other. It explains the origin of a local custom.
entries.9:20: Mordecai wrote letters to all the Jews throughout the empire, both near and far. It shows him organizing a shared celebration for everyone.
entries.9:21: He told them to celebrate the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar every year. It established an annual tradition.
entries.9:22: These were the days the Jews got relief from their enemies, and the month of sorrow became a month of joy, so they were to celebrate with feasting, gifts to each other, and gifts to the poor. It turns a painful memory into a yearly reminder of gratitude and generosity.
entries.9:23: The Jews agreed to keep doing this, just as Mordecai had instructed them in writing. It shows the community accepting the new tradition.
entries.9:24: Haman had plotted to destroy all the Jews and had cast lots (called Pur) to pick the day. It explains the background of the threat they had faced.
entries.9:25: When the king learned of the plot, he ordered that Haman's evil plan against the Jews fall on Haman himself, and Haman and his sons were hanged. It shows the plot backfiring on the one who made it.
entries.9:26: The days were named Purim after the word Pur, because of the letter and everything the Jews had seen and experienced. It explains where the holiday's name came from.
entries.9:27: The Jews made it a firm rule for themselves, their descendants, and anyone who joined them to keep these two days every year without fail. It shows the celebration became a lasting commitment.
entries.9:28: These days were to be remembered in every generation, family, region, and town, so that Purim would never be forgotten. It emphasizes how important it was to pass the memory down.
entries.9:29: Esther and Mordecai sent a second letter confirming the order about Purim with their full authority. It shows them making the celebration official.
entries.9:30: Mordecai sent letters to all the Jews across the hundred and twenty-seven provinces with words of peace and truth. It shows the message was meant to bring reassurance and unity.
entries.9:31: They established the days of Purim at their set times, just as Mordecai and Esther had ordered, along with the rules about fasting and crying out for help. It connects the celebration to the prayers and fasting that came before it.
entries.9:32: Esther's order made the rules about Purim official, and it was written down in the record book. It shows the tradition was formally recorded so it would last.
entries.10:1: The king taxed the whole empire, including distant islands, showing the reach of his power. It reminds us that rulers can demand much from ordinary people.
entries.10:2: The writer points readers to official royal records for the full account of the king's achievements and Mordecai's honor. It shows that Mordecai's rise was a real, recorded event, not a legend.
entries.10:3: Mordecai, a Jew, became the second most powerful man in the empire and used his position to help his people and bring them peace. It shows that God can place someone in high office to protect others.
